title: Comics industry timeline, 2012–2025: the events that shaped the market
answer: The years from 2012 to 2025 saw the founding of CBCS (2014), the biggest single-issue print run since 1993 (Star Wars #1, 2015), the deaths of Stan Lee and Steve Ditko (2018), the pandemic distribution shutdown (2020), Marvel and DC leaving Diamond (2020–2021), a run of record auction prices (2021–2024) and Diamond's bankruptcy (January 2025). This timeline lists the documented events that mattered for collectors, year by year.
body:
## 2012

- **March** — Image publishes Saga #1 by Brian K. Vaughan and Fiona Staples.
- **June** — DC's Before Watchmen prequels begin.
- **July** — The Walking Dead #100 is the best-selling comic of the year.
- **October** — Marvel NOW! relaunch begins.

## 2013

- **October** — DC Entertainment announces it will move its publishing operation from New York to Burbank, California.

## 2014

- CBCS (Comic Book Certification Service) is founded in Dallas by Steve Borock, formerly CGC's primary grader. See [CGC vs CBCS](/guides/cgc-vs-cbcs).
- **October** — Marvel's Thor #1 introduces Jane Foster as Thor.

## 2015

- **January** — Marvel's Star Wars #1 ships roughly a million copies, the largest single-issue print run since the early 1990s.
- **April** — DC completes its move to Burbank.
- **May** — Secret Wars begins; the Marvel line relaunches afterwards as All-New, All-Different Marvel.
- **September** — DC begins crediting Bill Finger as Batman's co-creator.

## 2016

- **May** — DC Universe: Rebirth #1 launches DC Rebirth.
- **May** — Riri Williams debuts in Invincible Iron Man #9. See [First appearance of Riri Williams](/guides/first-appearance-of-riri-williams).

## 2017

- **September** — Marvel Legacy relaunch. Len Wein, co-creator of Wolverine and Swamp Thing, dies on 10 September.

## 2018

- **April** — Action Comics #1000 is published.
- **June** — Steve Ditko, co-creator of Spider-Man and Doctor Strange, dies in New York.
- **November** — Stan Lee dies in Los Angeles on 12 November, aged 95. See [Stan Lee and the signed-comic market](/guides/stan-lee-signed-comics).
- Beckett Collectibles acquires CBCS.

## 2019

- **March** — Detective Comics #1000 is published, Batman's 80th anniversary year.
- **August** — Marvel Comics #1000 marks Marvel's 80th anniversary.

## 2020

- **March** — Diamond Comic Distributors halts all shipments as the COVID-19 pandemic closes shops; new comics stop for roughly two months.
- **June** — DC announces it will no longer distribute through Diamond, ending Diamond's near-monopoly on the direct market.

## 2021

- **January** — A CGC 9.4 Batman #1 sells for 2.22 million dollars at Heritage.
- **March** — Marvel announces its move to Penguin Random House for direct-market distribution, effective 1 October 2021.
- **April** — A CGC 8.5 Action Comics #1 sells for 3.25 million dollars via ComicConnect.
- **September** — A CGC 9.6 Amazing Fantasy #15 sells for 3.6 million dollars at Heritage, then a record for any comic.

## 2022

- **January** — A CGC 8.0 Detective Comics #27 sells for 1.5 million dollars at Heritage.
- **March** — A CGC 9.4 Marvel Comics #1 sells for 2.4 million dollars at Heritage.
- **April** — A CGC 9.4 Captain America Comics #1 sells for 3.12 million dollars at Heritage. Neal Adams dies on 28 April.
- **May** — George Pérez dies on 6 May.
- **December** — Heritage announces a private sale of a CGC 7.0 Superman #1 for 5.3 million dollars, a new record.

## 2023

- **June** — John Romita Sr., who designed the Punisher and Wolverine's costume, dies on 12 June.
- **October** — Keith Giffen dies.

## 2024

- **April** — A CGC 8.5 Action Comics #1 sells for 6 million dollars at Heritage, the current record. See [Record comic book sales](/guides/record-comic-book-sales).
- **October** — DC launches the Absolute Universe line.

## 2025

- **January** — Diamond Comic Distributors files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 14 January. See [The Diamond bankruptcy explained](/guides/diamond-comic-distributors-bankruptcy-2025).
- **May** — Peter David, writer of The Incredible Hulk for twelve years, dies on 24 May.
- **June** — Jim Shooter, Marvel's editor-in-chief from 1978 to 1987, dies on 30 June.

This timeline is limited to events that were publicly reported at the time and will be extended as the record grows.

title: The Diamond Comic Distributors bankruptcy (January 2025) explained
answer: Diamond Comic Distributors, for decades the near-exclusive distributor of comics to comic shops, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 14 January 2025 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Maryland. The filing followed the loss of its exclusive Marvel and DC business in 2020–2021 and years of falling volume, and its businesses were sold through the court-supervised process during 2025. For collectors the direct effects were on new-comic supply chains and retailers, not on back-issue values.
body:
## Background

Diamond, founded by Steve Geppi in 1982, became the sole distributor to the direct market in the mid-1990s after the distributor wars of 1994–1996 left it with exclusive deals with Marvel (from 1995), DC, Image and Dark Horse. For a quarter of a century almost every comic sold in a comic shop passed through Diamond.

## What changed

- **March 2020** — the pandemic shutdown, during which Diamond stopped shipping and DC experimented with other distributors.
- **June 2020** — DC left Diamond for Lunar Distribution.
- **October 2021** — Marvel moved to Penguin Random House; Diamond continued to carry Marvel only as a wholesaler buying from PRH.
- **2022–2023** — other publishers, including IDW and Dark Horse, followed to PRH.

With the two largest publishers gone, Diamond's volume fell sharply.

## The filing

On 14 January 2025 Diamond and affiliated companies, including Alliance Game Distributors and Diamond Select Toys, filed for Chapter 11. The company continued operating while it sought buyers, and its businesses were sold through the bankruptcy process during 2025.

## What it meant for collectors

- **Back issues and graded books were unaffected**; Diamond distributed new comics, not the secondary market.
- **Retailers** faced disruption, and some shops that depended on Diamond's terms closed.
- **Diamond's own products** — Previews catalogue, Diamond Select collectibles and exclusive variants — became collectible footnotes in their own right.

See [How Marvel and DC changed distribution in 2020–2021](/guides/marvel-dc-distribution-changes-2020-2021) and the [industry timeline](/guides/comics-industry-timeline-2012-2025).

title: How Marvel and DC changed comics distribution in 2020–2021
answer: In June 2020 DC Comics ended its relationship with Diamond Comic Distributors and began shipping to comic shops through Lunar Distribution (and, initially, UCS Comic Distributors). In March 2021 Marvel announced it would move to Penguin Random House, effective 1 October 2021, with Diamond reduced to a wholesaler. Together the two moves ended Diamond's 25-year near-monopoly on the direct market and set up its 2025 bankruptcy.
body:
## The trigger

When the COVID-19 pandemic closed shops in March 2020, Diamond stopped shipping new comics entirely. DC, unwilling to wait, arranged shipments through two new distributors formed by large online retailers — Lunar Distribution (DCBS) and UCS Comic Distributors (Midtown Comics) — in April 2020, and on 5 June 2020 announced it was leaving Diamond permanently.

## Marvel's move

On 25 March 2021 Marvel announced a multi-year exclusive agreement with Penguin Random House Publisher Services to distribute its comics, graphic novels and trade paperbacks to the direct market from 1 October 2021. Diamond, which had been Marvel's exclusive distributor since 1995, could continue to supply shops only by buying from PRH as a wholesaler.

## Who followed

Other publishers moved to PRH over the following two years, including IDW (2022) and Dark Horse (2023). Image and most smaller publishers stayed with Diamond for longer, and Lunar grew into a major distributor.

## Why it matters to collectors

- **New-comic supply** became split across several distributors with different terms, which changed how retailers ordered and how many copies of a new key ended up in the market.
- **Variants and exclusives** tied to Diamond's Previews catalogue declined.
- **Diamond's decline** led directly to its Chapter 11 filing in January 2025. See [The Diamond bankruptcy explained](/guides/diamond-comic-distributors-bankruptcy-2025).

Back issues and graded comics were not affected by any of this; the secondary market runs through auction houses, dealers and marketplaces such as this one.

title: Stan Lee (1922–2018) and the market for Stan Lee signed comics
answer: Stan Lee, born Stanley Lieber on 28 December 1922, co-created the Fantastic Four, Spider-Man, Hulk, Thor, Iron Man, the X-Men and the Avengers as Marvel's editor and writer, and died in Los Angeles on 12 November 2018, aged 95. In his last decade he signed enormous numbers of comics at conventions, many under CGC's Signature Series programme, so witnessed Stan Lee signatures are common; the value of a signed book depends on the book itself, the label, and the pairing of signer and issue.
body:
## Career in brief

Lee joined Timely Comics in 1939 as an assistant and became editor in 1941; his first credited work is a text story in Captain America Comics #3 (May 1941). After two decades of genre comics, he wrote Fantastic Four #1 with Jack Kirby in 1961 and, over the next five years, most of the Marvel Universe with Kirby, Steve Ditko, Don Heck, Bill Everett and John Romita Sr. He was Marvel's editor-in-chief until 1972, its publisher after that, and its public face for the rest of his life.

## The signing years

From the 2000s Lee appeared at conventions across the United States and signed comics, posters and memorabilia in volume, most of it witnessed by CGC or CBCS representatives and encapsulated with yellow labels. Tens of thousands of witnessed Stan Lee signatures exist.

## What a Stan Lee signature is worth

- **On a key he created** — Amazing Fantasy #15, Fantastic Four #1, X-Men #1 — a witnessed signature adds meaningfully to an already valuable book.
- **On a modern comic** — the signature is most of the value, and because so many exist, that value is modest.
- **On a book unrelated to him** — often neutral.

The supply of new witnessed signatures ended in November 2018, which supports prices at the top of the market but does not make every signed modern book scarce. See [What is a Signature Series comic?](/guides/what-is-a-signature-series-comic).

## Authenticity

Only a CGC yellow label, a CBCS yellow (witnessed) or red (authenticated) label, or documented provenance from a witnessed signing establishes a Lee signature. Unwitnessed signatures on raw books are common and frequently not genuine. See [What do CGC label colours mean?](/guides/what-do-cgc-label-colors-mean).

The [characters](/characters) Lee co-created each have a page on this site listing their first appearances and the copies in the store.
